reconstructed_theorem_text: Let iota be any finite index type and let E be the real Euclidean space indexed by iota, with its Euclidean norm and measurable structure. For every measure nu on E, every probability measure mu on E, every nonzero real eta, and every y,yprime in E, define Z_y = integral_E exp(-norm(z-y)^2/(2*eta)) dnu(z) and Z_yprime = integral_E exp(-norm(z-yprime)^2/(2*eta)) dnu(z). Define the real-valued spatial function r by r(t) = -norm(t-y)^2/(2*eta)-log(Z_y)-(-norm(t-yprime)^2/(2*eta))+log(Z_yprime). Then information(mu,1,r) = integral_E norm(gradient r(x))^2 dmu(x) = (eta^(-1))^2*norm(y-yprime)^2. Here information(base,q,r) is the integral against base of q(x) times the squared Euclidean norm of the spatial gradient of r, and the weight in this theorem is identically one. The assumptions are that iota is finite, mu has total mass one, and eta is nonzero. The measure nu is arbitrary and is used only in Z_y and Z_yprime; mu is the measure used to integrate the squared gradient. No equality or other relationship between nu and mu is required. Both normalizer logarithms are scalar constants with respect to the differentiation variable t. The statement is universally quantified over all the stated objects and concerns exactly this explicit function r. No positivity of eta, probability or sigma-finiteness assumption on nu, exponential-integrability assumption, or positivity of either normalizer is stated; the integral, logarithm, reciprocal, and powers retain their Lean real-operation meanings. The numerical coefficient is exactly (eta^(-1))^2. The answer depends only on eta and the squared distance between the centers, with no explicit dimension factor, no dependence on nu, and no dependence on the distribution of mu beyond its total mass one. This is an identity for the displayed Fisher functional, not an assertion identifying r as the log-likelihood ratio of specified measures.
